steps.title: Thiols and pyrazines
steps.body: Marlborough Sauvignon's tropical notes come from thiols, like 3MH and 3MHA, which smell of passion fruit and grapefruit; they're released during fermentation. Green notes, grass and green pepper, come from methoxypyrazines, kept by cool nights. Marlborough grapes have unusually high levels of both, which explains the intensity.

steps.title: Winemaking
steps.body: Machine harvesting at night breaks some skins, releasing thiol precursors; cool, protective fermentation in steel with selected yeasts keeps them. No oak and early bottling preserve freshness. Some producers make wild-yeast, barrel-fermented or lees-aged versions for texture, but the classic style is pure and pungent.

steps.prompt: Which compounds give Marlborough Sauvignon its passion fruit aroma?

steps.title: Wairau and Awatere
steps.body: The Wairau Valley, broad and warmer, on stony and silty soils, gives the classic ripe, tropical style. The Awatere Valley, to the south-east, higher, drier, cooler and windier, gives more herbal, mineral, saline wines with tomato leaf and green notes. Many producers blend both for balance.

steps.prompt: Which help create the Marlborough style?

steps.title: What you learned
points: Thiols give passion fruit; pyrazines give grass
Machine harvest and cool steel fermentation preserve aromas
Wairau is tropical; Awatere herbal and saline
